note: Anthropologists of the 19th and early 20th centuries sorted people into 'races' and 'types'. Later research found that most human genetic variation lies within populations: Lewontin (1972) put that share at about 85%, and Rosenberg and colleagues (2002) at 93 to 95%. Differences between populations build up gradually with geographic distance (Serre and Pääbo 2004; Rosenberg and colleagues 2005), so head shape, stature and skin colour do not sort people into a few fixed types, and Boas (1912) found that even the cephalic index of immigrants' children born in the United States differed from their parents'. The American Association of Physical Anthropologists' Statement on Race and Racism (2019) concludes that humans do not fall biologically into separate continental types or genetic race clusters, and that the idea of race arose from, and served, European colonialism, oppression and discrimination. Several of the authors quoted here ranked the groups they described, and their portraits were made to illustrate 'types'; they are shown here only as records of that history.

nw_europe.title: Northern and western Europe
nw_europe.text: Ripley (1899) gave the north-west of Europe to his 'Teutonic' type: long head and face, very light hair, blue eyes, tall stature and a narrow nose. Deniker (1900) described much the same people as a 'Northern race', with an average height of 1.73 m and a cephalic index (head breadth as a percentage of head length) of 76 to 79, and placed it in Scandinavia, northern Britain, the northern Netherlands and the Baltic provinces. Coon (1939) kept the name 'Nordic' but called it a partly depigmented branch of the 'Mediterranean' stock.

images.title: Cephalic index of Europe
images.caption: William Z. Ripley, map of the cephalic index, The Races of Europe (1899). Darker shading marks broader, shorter heads (index up to 87–89); the lighter British Isles, Scandinavia and Iberia mark the long-headed populations he called Teutonic and Mediterranean.
images.author: William Z. Ripley

images.title: 'Dane, Nordic'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate XI, 2: a Danish man captioned 'Dane (Nordic)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

ce_europe.title: Central and eastern Europe
ce_europe.text: Ripley (1899) drew a belt of his 'Alpine' type, which other writers called Celtic or Slavic, across central Europe from France through the Alps and Austria-Hungary towards Russia: round head, broad face, medium and stocky build, light chestnut hair and hazel-grey eyes. Deniker (1900) added a fair, rather short 'Eastern race' (about 1.63 to 1.64 m, cephalic index 82 to 83) among White Russians (Belarusians) and some Lithuanians, and a 'Vistulian' sub-race among Poles. His map of 1899 shows the region as a patchwork of principal and secondary races.

images.title: Deniker's map of Europe
images.caption: Joseph Deniker's map 'Races de l'Europe', reprinted by Ripley in the Journal of the Anthropological Institute (1899). The legend lists six principal races (Nordic, Littoral, Oriental, Adriatic or Dinaric, Ibero-Insular, Occidental or Cévenole) and four secondary ones.
images.author: Joseph Deniker

images.title: 'Alpine type', Austria
images.caption: Ripley, The Races of Europe (1899), plate 'The three European racial types', figs. 21–22: an Austrian man captioned 'Alpine type. Blue eyes, brown hair. Index 88.'
images.author: William Z. Ripley

s_europe.title: Southern Europe
s_europe.text: Ripley (1899) assigned the Mediterranean shores to a 'Mediterranean' type: long-headed and long-faced like his northern type, but with dark brown or black hair, dark eyes and a medium, slender build. Deniker (1900) split the south into a very short, long-headed 'Ibero-insular race' (1.61 to 1.62 m, index 73 to 76) in Iberia and the western Mediterranean islands, a taller 'Littoral' race along the coasts, and an 'Adriatic or Dinaric race' (1.68 to 1.72 m, index 85 to 86) whose purest examples he placed in Bosnia, Dalmatia and Croatia. Ripley also placed round-headed 'Alpine' populations in northern Italy, above all in Piedmont.

images.title: 'Catalan, Iberian'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate XII, 1: 'Catalan man, Spain (Iberian)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

images.title: 'Alpine type', Piedmont
images.caption: Ripley, 'The Racial Geography of Europe: Italy', Popular Science Monthly 51 (October 1897): a young man from Piedmont, front and profile, captioned 'Alpine type', cephalic index 91.3. The same photographs are figs. 79–80 of The Races of Europe (1899).
images.author: William Z. Ripley

mena.title: Middle East, North Africa and the Caucasus
mena.text: Most 19th-century schemes put North Africa and Western Asia inside a broad 'Caucasian' race, a name Blumenbach (1795) took from the Caucasus, partly because he held its Georgians to be the most beautiful people; his model skull for it was a Georgian woman's. The Meyers Konversations-Lexikon (1885–90) split that race into 'Aryans', 'Hamites' and 'Semites', names taken from language families, and Deniker (1900) described an 'Arab or Semite race', a 'Berber race' with four sub-types, and an 'Assyroid' type among Hadjemi Persians, some Kurdish tribes and some Armenians and Jews, described mainly by the shape of the nose. Keane's Man, Past and Present (1920 edition) labelled the Beja peoples of Sudan 'Hamite'.

images.title: 'Verbreitung der Menschenrassen'
images.caption: 'Ethnographische Karte: Verbreitung der Menschenrassen' (distribution of human races), Meyers Konversations-Lexikon, 4th edition (1885–90). The legend divides humanity into a 'Caucasian', a 'Mongolian' and a 'Negroid' race, with 'Dravidians and Sinhalese' marked as uncertain.
images.author: Bibliographisches Institut, Leipzig

images.title: Blumenbach's five skulls
images.caption: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach, De generis humani varietate nativa, 3rd edition (1795), plate II: skulls labelled Tungusae, Caribaei, Feminae Georgianae, O-taheitae and Aethiopissae, which stood for his Mongolian, American, Caucasian, Malay and Ethiopian varieties. The Georgian woman's skull in the middle was his model for the 'Caucasian' variety.
images.author: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach

images.title: 'Bisharin, Hamite'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate XIII, 1–2: 'Bisharin, Egyptian Sudan (Hamite)', profile and front.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

ssa.title: Sub-Saharan Africa
ssa.text: Blumenbach (1795) called the peoples of Africa south of the Sahara the 'Ethiopian' variety, and Keane (1899) made the 'Ethiopic' one of his four primary divisions of humanity, openly ranking it the lowest and the 'Caucasic' the highest. Deniker (1900), who sorted races first by hair form and then by skin colour, nose and stature, divided the region among a 'Negro' race (with 'Nigritian' and 'Bantu' sub-races), a short 'Negrillo' sub-race, a 'Bushman' race and an 'Ethiopian' race of north-east Africa. Bettany's map (1888) drew similar borders between 'Hamites', 'Ethiopians', 'Negroes', 'Bantu' and others.

images.title: 'Afrikanische Völker'
images.caption: Gustav Mützel, plate 'Afrikanische Völker' (African peoples), Meyers Konversations-Lexikon, 4th edition, vol. 1 (1885–90): 30 numbered portraits labelled by people, from Moroccan Arabs and Copts to Zulu, Akka and Somali.
images.author: Gustav Mützel for Meyers Konversations-Lexikon

images.title: Bettany's map of Africa
images.caption: G. T. Bettany, The World's Inhabitants (1888), ch. XI 'Distribution of African Races', p. 685: map with its own labels 'Hamites', 'Ethiopians', 'Fulbs', 'Negroes', 'Bantu', 'Hottentots' and 'Hovas'.
images.author: G. T. Bettany

images.title: 'Shilluk, Nilote'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate XIII, 6: 'Shilluk, Egyptian Sudan (Nilote)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

s_asia.title: South Asia
s_asia.text: Herbert Risley's The People of India (1908) sorted the population of British India into seven 'types', among them 'Turko-Iranian', 'Indo-Aryan', 'Dravidian' and 'Mongoloid', by head shape, stature, complexion and especially the nasal index (nose breadth as a percentage of nose height). Risley claimed that the castes he measured in Hindustan and Bihar fell in much the same order by nasal index as by social precedence. Deniker (1900) described an 'Indo-Afghan race' among Afghans, Rajputs and Brahmins and a 'Dravidian race' in the south, while the Meyers map (1885–90) left 'Dravidians and Sinhalese' in an uncertain position.

images.title: Gurkha, fig. 125
images.caption: Deniker, The Races of Man (1900), fig. 125: 'Gurkha of the Kus or Khas tribe, Nepal; mixed Indo-Thibetan type'.
images.author: Joseph Deniker

images.title: 'Afghan, Iranian'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate XII, 6: 'Afghan of Zerafshan (Iranian)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

c_asia.title: Central Asia
c_asia.text: Deniker (1900) described a 'Turkish' or 'Turco-Tatar' race that he called fairly pure among the Kirghiz and the Tatars of Astrakhan and mixed with other races among Turkmen and Ottoman Turks. Ripley (1899), drawing on measurements by Ujfalvy and Topinard, claimed that the mountain Tajiks (Galchas) of the Pamir, grey-eyed, dark-haired, stocky and with cephalic indexes mostly above 86, matched his European 'Alpine' type almost exactly, and took this as a sign that round-headed Europeans came from Asia. Keane's book (1920 edition) still labelled Tajiks 'Alpine'.

images.title: 'Tajik, Alpine'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate XIV, 5: 'Tajik woman of E. Turkestan (Alpine)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

images.title: Kundrof Tatar, fig. 107
images.caption: Deniker, The Races of Man (1900), fig. 107: 'Kundrof Tatar (Turkoman) of Astrakhan, with cap', one of his examples of the Turkish race.
images.author: Joseph Deniker

e_asia.title: East Asia
e_asia.text: Blumenbach (1795) grouped the peoples of East and North Asia as the 'Mongolian' variety, one of his five, and illustrated it with a skull labelled 'Tungusae' (a Tungus). Deniker (1900) split his 'Mongol race' into a northern sub-race with oval or round faces and prominent cheekbones (Manchuria, Korea, northern China, Mongolia) and a southern one with lozenge-shaped or square faces (southern China and Indo-China), and treated the Ainu of northern Japan as a race of their own.

images.title: Blumenbach's five skulls
images.caption: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach, De generis humani varietate nativa, 3rd edition (1795), plate II: skulls labelled Tungusae, Caribaei, Feminae Georgianae, O-taheitae and Aethiopissae, which stood for his Mongolian, American, Caucasian, Malay and Ethiopian varieties.

images.title: Leao-yu-chow, fig. 119
images.caption: Deniker, The Races of Man (1900), fig. 119: 'Leao-yu-chow, Chinese woman, born at Foo-chow, eighteen years old, height 1m. 52', cited for his southern Mongol sub-race.
images.author: Joseph Deniker

se_asia.title: Southeast Asia
se_asia.text: Blumenbach (1795) created a fifth, 'Malay' variety for the peoples of the Malay world and the Pacific islands. Deniker (1900) placed northern Vietnam in his southern 'Mongol' sub-race and described an 'Indonesian race' among Dayaks, Bataks and others in the archipelago, while both he and Keane set apart the Semang, the Aeta and the Andaman islanders as 'Negritos', a group defined mainly by short stature and tightly curled ('woolly') hair.

images.title: Tong King artisan, fig. 121
images.caption: Deniker, The Races of Man (1900), fig. 121: 'Tong King artisan of Son-tai, twenty-three years old', cited for his southern Mongol sub-race.
images.author: Joseph Deniker

images.title: 'Semang, Negrito'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate II, 2: 'Semang, Malay Peninsula (Negrito)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

oceania.title: Oceania
oceania.text: Huxley (1870) grouped Aboriginal Australians under an 'Australioid' type, and the Meyers plate of Oceanic peoples (1885–90) arranged its portraits under the headings Australians, Melanesians, Micronesians and Polynesians. Deniker (1900) separated an 'Australian' race, a 'Melanesian' race with a 'Papuan' sub-race in New Guinea, which he told apart from African groups by less tightly curled hair and lighter skin, and a 'Polynesian' race found from Hawaii to New Zealand.

images.title: 'Ozeanische Völker'
images.caption: Plate 'Ozeanische Völker' (Oceanic peoples), Meyers Konversations-Lexikon, 4th edition, vol. 12 (1885–90): 30 numbered portraits grouped as Australier, Melanesier, Mikronesier and Polynesier. The face of no. 1 is torn in this scan.
images.author: Bibliographisches Institut, Leipzig

images.title: 'Kiwai, Papuan'
images.caption: Keane, Man, Past and Present, revised edition (1920), plate III, 4: 'Native of Oromosapua, Kiwai, British New Guinea (Papuan)'.
images.author: A. H. Keane, revised by A. Hingston Quiggin and A. C. Haddon

americas.title: The Americas
americas.text: For the Americas these schemes described the Indigenous peoples; people of European, African or Asian descent were counted under their ancestors' 'races'. Blumenbach (1795) made Indigenous Americans the 'American' variety, and Samuel Morton's Crania Americana (1839) measured skull volume, concluded that all American nations except the 'Polar tribes' formed one race, and attached claims about mental character to it. Deniker (1900) instead listed four races, North American, Central American, South American and Patagonian, separated by stature, head shape and hair, while the Meyers map (1885–90) put 'Americans' inside its 'Mongolian race'.

images.title: 'Amerikanische Völker'
images.caption: Gustav Mützel, plate 'Amerikanische Völker' (American peoples), Meyers Konversations-Lexikon, 4th edition, vol. 1 (1885–90): 33 numbered portraits from the Aleuts and Inuit to the Mapuche and Fuegians.
images.author: Gustav Mützel for Meyers Konversations-Lexikon

images.title: Kalina (Carib), fig. 167
images.caption: Deniker, The Races of Man (1900), fig. 167: 'Kalina or Carib of Dutch Guiana', cited for the straight-haired sub-race of his South American race.
images.author: Joseph Deniker
